turns.prompt_text: What is this bendy strip of metal and where can I buy some? Attached 1 file. - 6f9811c6-c02a-458a-a65e-851ca65acc43
turns.response_html:
That bendy strip of metal is the 8-inch flexible straw specifically found on the WD-40 EZ-REACH can.

What is it?

Unlike standard plastic straws that are straight and flimsy, this is a flexible metal straw designed to bend and keep its shape. This allows you to snake the nozzle into tight or awkward spaces (like engine bays or under sinks) and spray with precision without needing to hold the straw in place with your other hand.

Where can you buy it?

Because the straw is permanently attached to the "Smart Straw" nozzle system, you generally have to buy the specific WD-40 EZ-REACH can rather than just the straw itself.

You can find it at most major hardware and home improvement stores:

  • Home Depot: Usually in stock for around $13.63 for a 14.4 oz can.
  • Walmart: Available in single cans or multi-packs.
  • Northern Tool: Sells the 14.4 oz model for approximately $13.99.
  • Office Depot/OfficeSupply.com: Often stocked in the maintenance or cleaning sections.

While you can buy generic plastic replacement straw kits (like those from Aeroflex) that fit standard aerosol cans, they do not have the "stay-put" metal memory of the EZ-REACH version.

turns.prompt_text: Do those exist separate? Where do they where does the WD-40 manufacturer get a hold of these?
turns.response_html:
Those bendy metal straws aren't typically sold as standalone consumer products by WD-40, but the component itself is a very specific industrial item.

1. What are they called?

In the manufacturing world, that "bendy strip" is known as Gooseneck Tubing (or sometimes Stay-Put or Interlocked Flexible Metal Tubing).

It is essentially a thin strip of stainless steel or galvanized steel that is wound in a way that creates high friction between the coils. This friction is what allows it to "remember" the shape you bend it into, unlike a standard spring or plastic tube.

2. Where does WD-40 get them?

WD-40 doesn't actually make the metal tubing themselves. They source it from specialized industrial manufacturers that produce "micro-gooseneck" tubing.

  • The Likely Suppliers: While WD-40 keeps their specific contractors private, the major global players for this specific micro-tubing are companies like Hagitec (Japan), Uniprise International (USA), and Whitehouse Flexible Tubing (UK).
  • The Integration: The tubing is then sent to a nozzle manufacturer (like Aptar or Precision Valve Corporation) who over-molds the plastic "Smart Straw" cap onto the metal tube to create the finished EZ-REACH lid.

3. Can you buy them separately?

You won't find them at a typical hardware store next to the duct tape, but you can get them through two specific "secret" channels:

  • Pest Control Suppliers: This is the best place for "consumer-ready" versions. Companies like 1Env or Lance Lab sell "Flexible Aerosol Straw Kits." These are designed for pest control professionals to snake foam into wall crevices. They come with an adapter that fits onto standard aerosol cans.
  • Industrial Parts Houses: If you just want the raw bendy metal (no nozzle), you can find it at McMaster-Carr or Grainger by searching for "Gooseneck" or "Positionable Coolant Hoses."

One quick warning: If you're planning to swap a WD-40 EZ-REACH lid onto a different can (like spray paint), be careful. Different brands use different valve stems (male vs. female), and the chemical propellant in spray paint can sometimes clog the fine internal channel of the metal straw much faster than a lubricant would.

turns.prompt_text: All right. I got another question. What is silicone?
turns.response_html:
Silicone is essentially a "hybrid" material—a synthetic polymer that bridges the gap between organic chemistry (like plastics) and inorganic chemistry (like glass). It is prized for being incredibly durable, heat-resistant, and chemically "lazy" (it doesn't like to react with things).

1. The Chemistry: Silicon vs. Silicone

It’s easy to mix them up, but they are very different things.

  • Silicon (no 'e'): This is a natural chemical element ($Si$) found in sand and quartz. It’s a hard, brittle metalloid used to make computer chips.
  • Silicone (with an 'e'): This is a man-made polymer. Scientists take silicon atoms and link them with oxygen atoms to create a "siloxane" backbone: $[R_2SiO]_n$.

By attaching different organic groups (the "$R$" in the formula, usually methyl groups), engineers can change the material's texture from a thin liquid to a thick gel or a tough, rubbery solid.

2. Why is it so popular?

Silicone has a set of "superpowers" that make it better than natural rubber or standard plastics in many scenarios:

  • Thermal Stability: It can handle extreme temperatures, typically from -55°C to over 300°C, without melting or becoming brittle.
  • Water Repellency: It is highly hydrophobic, which is why it's the gold standard for bathroom caulk and waterproof seals.
  • Bio-compatibility: It’s generally non-toxic and doesn't support bacterial growth, making it safe for food-grade kitchenware and medical implants.
  • Low Conductivity: It’s an excellent electrical insulator, which is why it's used to coat wires and protect sensitive electronics.

3. The Different "States" of Silicone

Because the chemistry is so flexible, silicone shows up in three main forms:

FormCommon Uses
Fluids / OilsLubricants, hydraulic fluids, and even ingredients in some hair conditioners and cosmetics.
ResinsHigh-heat coatings, water-repellent paints, and industrial varnishes.
Elastomers (Rubber)O-rings, gaskets, kitchen spatulas, phone cases, and medical tubing.

4. Where you'll see it every day

  • In your kitchen: Those flexible, colorful muffin tins and spatulas. Unlike plastic, they won't leach chemicals into your food at high heat.
  • In your car: It’s in the spark plug wires and the gaskets that keep oil from leaking out of the engine.
  • In construction: The clear, rubbery "goo" used to seal windows or the edges of a bathtub to prevent leaks.
  • In electronics: It’s used as a "potting compound" to encase circuit boards, protecting them from vibration and moisture.

In short, if you need a material that stays flexible when it's freezing, doesn't melt when it's hot, and won't rot or degrade over time, silicone is usually the answer.

Does that help clear up the "what" and "why" behind it?

turns.prompt_text: That helps quite a bit. I imagine it's also used in like health or clothing things as it seems to be at least non-toxic to humans over a long period of time.
turns.response_html:
You’ve hit the nail on the head. Because silicone is chemically inert—meaning it doesn't like to react with other substances—it is the "gold standard" for anything that needs to sit against (or inside) the human body for a long time.

1. Silicone in Healthcare (Biocompatibility)

In medicine, "biocompatible" means the body doesn't see the material as a foreign invader and try to attack it. This makes silicone indispensable:

  • Implants & Prosthetics: From heart valves and joint replacements to aesthetic implants, silicone can stay in the body for decades without degrading or causing toxic reactions.
  • Tubing & Catheters: It is used for IV lines and catheters because it is soft, flexible, and—crucially—does not support the growth of bacteria as easily as organic rubber.
  • Contact Lenses: "Silicone hydrogel" lenses are popular because they allow much more oxygen to pass through the lens to your cornea than older plastic materials, keeping eyes healthier.

2. Silicone in Clothing & Textiles

In the fashion world, silicone is used more for its physical "grip" and durability than just its safety:

  • Anti-Slip Grips: If you’ve ever worn "stay-up" stockings, strapless bras, or cycling shorts, that rubbery clear strip on the inside that keeps the fabric from sliding down is almost always silicone.
  • Screen Printing: High-quality "puffy" or 3D logos on t-shirts are often made with silicone ink. It’s more expensive than plastic-based (plastisol) ink, but it won't crack or peel, even after hundreds of washes.
  • Performance Gear: Silicone coatings are used on professional swimwear to reduce "drag" in the water and on outdoor gear to provide a permanent, breathable waterproof layer.

3. Is it truly "Non-Toxic"?

For the most part, yes. Unlike many plastics, silicone:

  1. Does not contain BPA or Phthalates: These are the "endocrine disruptors" people worry about leaching into food or skin.
  2. Does not "Off-gas": It doesn't release volatile organic compounds (VOCs) into the air like some foams and plastics do.
  3. Is Heat Stable: It won't melt or release fumes at any temperature a human could survive in.

The "But": While the solid form is incredibly safe, liquid silicone (like some industrial sprays or low-quality lubricants) can occasionally cause skin irritation or, in rare medical cases, "silicone granulomas" if it migrates into tissue as a liquid. But for the "bendy" solid stuff you see every day, it's about as safe as a material gets.

turns.prompt_text: What are some weight at home ways I could make things out of silicone.
turns.response_html:
Making things out of silicone at home is surprisingly accessible, ranging from "kitchen science" experiments to more professional-grade engineering. Since you have a 3D printer and an interest in DIY electronics, you’re actually in a perfect position to bridge the gap between digital design and physical rubber parts.

Here are the three best "at-home" methods for working with silicone:

1. The "Oogoo" Method (DIY Putty)

This is the cheapest, most "right-at-home" way to make silicone parts. Oogoo is a homemade substitute for Sugru (a moldable glue).

  • Ingredients: 100% Silicone Caulk (the kind that smells like vinegar) and Cornstarch.
  • The Process: You mix roughly equal parts caulk and cornstarch. The cornstarch provides internal moisture that makes the silicone cure in minutes rather than days.
  • Best For:
    • Making quick protective bumpers for electronics.
    • Custom grips for tools or pens.
    • Simple, hand-pressed molds of small objects.
  • Pro Tip: Add a drop of oil-based paint or a tiny bit of acrylic paint to color it.

2. The "3D Print to Silicone" Workflow

Since you have a Bambu Lab A1, this is likely your most powerful option. Instead of printing a final part, you print a negative mold.

  • The Process:
    1. Design a "box" in CAD that has the cavity of the object you want.
    2. Print the mold in PLA or PETG.
    3. Spray the inside with a mold release (even a light mist of cooking spray works in a pinch).
    4. Pour in a Two-Part Liquid Silicone (like Smooth-On or generic "Dragon Skin" alternatives).
  • Best For:
    • Custom gaskets or seals.
    • Soft robotic parts (if you're feeling ambitious with your Raspberry Pi).
    • High-precision enclosures for DIY sensors.

3. Two-Part Silicone Putty

If you want high detail without the mess of liquids, you can buy two-part "kneadable" silicone putty.

  • The Process: It comes with two tubs (Part A and Part B). You take an equal amount of each, mash them together like Play-Doh until the color is uniform, and then press it over an object. It usually sets in about 20 minutes.
  • Best For:
    • Taking quick impressions of existing parts or textures.
    • Creating "over-molds" on 3D prints to give them a soft-touch finish.

Comparison of Methods

MethodDifficultyCostPrecision
Oogoo (Caulk)EasyVery LowLow
Liquid PouringMediumModerateVery High
PuttyVery EasyModerateHigh

A Few "Jarvis-Approved" Safety Tips:

  • The Vinegar Smell: If you use the caulk method (Acetic Acid cure), it will smell strongly of vinegar. Ventilation is mandatory. Do it near an open window or under a range hood.
  • Inhibition: "Platinum-cure" silicones (the fancy liquid ones) are very sensitive. They will refuse to cure if they touch certain materials, specifically latex or sulfur-based clays. Always use nitrile gloves, not latex.
  • Bubble Trouble: When pouring liquid silicone, pour it in a very thin stream from about a foot above the mold. This "stretches" the bubbles until they pop before they hit the mold.

Are you thinking of making a specific part for your electronics projects, or just looking to add a "soft-touch" to some of your 3D prints?

turns.prompt_text: I'm just looking for different ways to manufacture things and I think silicon is a tool I need the tool set. Could I pick some up at Menards?
turns.response_html:
You can definitely find the materials for your "tool set" at Menards. Since you are interested in manufacturing and DIY, you'll likely want to pick up items for both the "Oogoo" method and more structured mold-making.

What to buy at Menards

The most versatile item to grab is 100% Silicone Sealant. When choosing a tube, look for Silicone I (or "All-Purpose") rather than Silicone II. Silicone I releases acetic acid (the vinegar smell) as it cures, which reacts much better with cornstarch if you want to make "Oogoo" putty.

  • 100% Silicone Caulk: Look for DAP Silicone Sealant or GE All Purpose Silicone 1. Menards typically stocks these in the paint and caulk aisle.
  • Cornstarch: Found in the grocery aisle, this is what you'll mix with the caulk to create a moldable putty that cures quickly.
  • Caulk Gun: If you don't already have one, you'll need a basic manual dripless caulk gun to get the silicone out of the tube.

Higher-Precision Options

While Menards is great for "hardware store hacks," they typically do not carry professional two-part liquid silicones (like for pouring detailed molds). For those, you would need to look at specialized craft or industrial suppliers.

Recommended "Tool Set" Additions

If you want to move beyond the caulk method for higher-fidelity parts (like those gaskets for your 3D prints), consider these specialized kits:

  • For High Detail: The Alumilite Amazing Mold Maker is a platinum-based silicone that picks up incredible detail and is even FDA-compliant if you ever wanted to make food-safe molds.
  • For Beginners: The Smooth-On Pourable Silicone Starter Kit is a classic entry point into professional mold making, providing everything you need to pour your first two-piece block mold.

If you're planning to use your Bambu Lab A1 to print molds for these materials, I can help you find the best Mold Release Spray to ensure your silicone parts don't get stuck in your 3D prints. Would you like me to look those up for you?

turns.prompt_text: Would any of these work? Attached 1 file. - abb2b897-c7a4-42c3-9baa-109364c3f8c9
turns.response_html:
Based on the image you shared from Menards, here is the breakdown of what will work for your at-home manufacturing projects:

The Short Answer:

Most of the ones in your photo are actually not ideal for the "Oogoo" (cornstarch) method.

  • Avoid the "Latex Ultra": This is a water-based acrylic/latex blend, not pure silicone. It will not work for making rubber parts.
  • Avoid "GE Supreme Silicone": These are neutral-cure silicones. While they are high-quality for sealing a bathtub, they lack the acetic acid (vinegar smell) needed to react with cornstarch to create a fast-curing putty.
  • White Lightning Silicone Ultra: These are marketed as "Low Odor," which almost always indicates a neutral cure that will stay gooey for too long when mixed with starch.

What to look for at Menards instead

For the Oogoo method, you want the "old-school" stuff that smells strongly of vinegar. At Menards, look for:

  1. GE All-Purpose Silicone 1 (Blue Label): This is the classic "acetoxy cure" silicone. It is explicitly what most DIYers use because the acetic acid reacts perfectly with the moisture in cornstarch to cure the part in minutes.
  2. Standard "Contractor Grade" 100% Silicone: Often the cheapest 100% silicone tube on the shelf is the one you want. Look at the back of the tube—if it has a warning about "Acetic Acid" vapors or tells you to wear gloves because it can irritate skin, that’s the one.

Pro Tips for Your "Manufacturing" Toolset:

  • Clear vs. White: Always grab the Clear version if you plan on adding colors (like oil paint or pigment). The White version is opaque and will make your colors look like pastels.
  • 3D Printing Molds: Since you have a Bambu Lab A1, you can print a mold, but remember that silicone hates certain materials. If you use the "Silicone 1" (acetoxy), it will peel right off of a PLA or PETG 3D print without much trouble, but a light wipe of vegetable oil or vaseline inside the mold helps ensure it doesn't stick.
  • The Smell: Since you're a veteran and likely used to working with industrial gear, just a heads-up—do not underestimate the vinegar smell of "Silicone 1" when mixing it. Do it in your garage or near an open window.

Quick Check: Did you see a blue-labeled "Silicone 1" tube nearby, or is this shelf all the "Supreme" and "Advanced" versions?

turns.prompt_text: It is all Supreme and advanced versions, unfortunately.
turns.response_html:
That is the classic "too much technology" problem—those "Supreme" and "Advanced" versions (Silicone 2) are engineered to be low-odor and fast-drying for bathrooms, but that actually breaks the chemistry for the DIY manufacturing you want to do.

Since you're at Menards, here is your "Plan B" to find the right stuff:

1. Check the Tile/Flooring Aisle

Don't look in the Paint/Caulk section. Walk over to the Tile & Flooring department. Look for:

  • TEC AccuColor 100 (100% Silicone): This is often used for grouting tile joints. It is almost always a "standard" acetoxy-cure silicone (the vinegar-smelling kind).
  • The "Cheapest" Option: Look for a brand like White Lightning or a generic Menards house brand that simply says "100% Silicone." If it's the cheapest tube there ($5–$7 range) and it doesn't say "Paintable in 30 minutes" or "Low Odor," it's likely the one you need.

2. Look for "Window & Door" (Blue Label)

If you see any GE tubes with a Blue Label that say "All Purpose Silicone 1," grab those. The "Supreme" (Red) and "Advanced" (Green) are the ones to avoid for Oogoo.

3. The "Back of the Tube" Test

Pick up a tube and look at the fine print on the back under "Warnings" or "Cleanup."

  • YES: If it says "Releases Acetic Acid during cure" or "Clean up with Mineral Spirits."
  • NO: If it says "Releases Ammonia/Alcohol" or "Water Cleanup."

Why you should hold out:

If you try to mix "Supreme" silicone with cornstarch, it will likely turn into a oily, curdled mess that never actually turns into rubber. It’s better to leave Menards empty-handed and hit a Hy-Vee or a small Ace Hardware for the basic GE Silicone 1.

Quick Tip for your 3D printer: If you can't find the right silicone today, you can still print your molds! Just make sure your walls are at least 2–3mm thick so they don't warp when you eventually pack the silicone putty into them.

Did you happen to see a "Blue Label" GE tube tucked away in a corner?

turns.prompt_text: Already I found some gorilla brand 100% all-purpose silicone
turns.response_html:
That is a perfect find. Gorilla Brand 100% Silicone is widely considered the "gold standard" for the Oogoo method because it’s a high-strength acetoxy-cure silicone.

Why Gorilla works for this:

Unlike the "Supreme" or "Advanced" versions you saw earlier, Gorilla’s all-purpose formula is designed to be incredibly tough and flexible. Once you mix it with cornstarch, it will cure into a high-grade synthetic rubber that feels professional, not like cheap caulk.

The "Oogoo" Manufacturing Guide

Since you’re adding this to your toolset, here is the quick "formula" to get started:

  1. The Ratio: Start with 1 part cornstarch to 1 part silicone (by volume).
    • More starch = faster cure and stiffer rubber.
    • Less starch = slower cure and more flexible/stretchy rubber.
  2. The Mix: Squeeze the silicone into a disposable cup, add the starch, and mix like crazy. It will start out sticky, then turn into a dough-like consistency.
  3. Working Time: You have about 5 to 10 minutes before it starts to skin over. Work fast!
  4. Cure Time: It should be fully "rubbery" and handleable in about 30 to 60 minutes, though it reaches full strength in 24 hours.

Tips for your 3D-Printed Molds

Since you have the Bambu Lab A1, you can really level up your parts:

  • Print in PLA: Silicone won't bond to PLA, making it easy to pop out.
  • Thin Walls: If you are making a mold, print it with 2–3 wall loops. The Oogoo putty requires some pressure to pack into the corners, and you don't want the mold to crack.
  • Surface Finish: Use a 0.08mm or 0.12mm layer height for your mold. Silicone picks up everything—if your print has visible layer lines, your final rubber part will have them too.

One Final Warning

When you crack that Gorilla tube open, you're going to get a very strong hit of vinegar smell. That’s the acetic acid reacting with the air. It’s totally normal, but it will linger in a room for a few hours, so definitely do your mixing in a well-ventilated spot.

Are you planning to try a hand-molded "Oogoo" project first, or are you heading straight for a 3D-printed mold?

turns.prompt_text: Do a small test Republic first.
turns.response_html:
A wise move, sir. In engineering, a "Minimum Viable Product" test is always preferable to wasting a full tube of Gorilla Silicone on a failed experiment. Assuming you meant a "test run," let's establish a quick protocol to calibrate your technique.

The "Oogoo" Calibration Test

For your first batch, don't worry about a 3D-printed mold just yet. Let's aim for a simple "test puck" to get a feel for the curing time and final texture.

The Equipment:

  • A small disposable cup (or a scrap of cardboard).
  • A popsicle stick or plastic spoon (disposable is key; silicone is a nightmare to clean).
  • Gorilla 100% Silicone and Cornstarch.
  • Nitrile gloves (unless you want "gorilla hands" for the next three days).

The Protocol

  1. The Drop: Squeeze a dollop of silicone about the size of a golf ball into your cup.
  2. The Catalyst: Add an roughly equal volume of cornstarch on top.
  3. The Integration: Mix aggressively. It will initially look like breadcrumbs, then suddenly turn into a smooth, dough-like putty.
    • Note: If it stays too sticky to handle, add a pinch more starch.
  4. The "Squish" Test: Take the ball out and flatten it onto a surface (like the back of a spare 3D print or a piece of wax paper).
  5. The Observation:
    • At 5 minutes: It should still be moldable but starting to feel "firm."
    • At 15 minutes: It should be "tack-free" (you can touch it without it sticking to your finger).
    • At 60 minutes: It should be fully rubberized.

Evaluating the Results

Once it's cured, try to tear it. You’ll notice the Gorilla Silicone provides an impressive tensile strength. If it's too brittle, you used too much starch; if it's too floppy, you need more.

Once you’ve mastered the "feel" of the mix, we can move on to your Bambu Lab A1 and design a proper mold for your electronics enclosures.

Shall I prepare a few design tips for your first 3D-printed silicone mold, or would you like to focus on the chemistry for now?

turns.prompt_text: Well this cornstarch work? Attached 1 file. - 58399ba0-0352-4ce2-9658-453e2269c731
turns.response_html:
Yes, that will work perfectly.

Clabber Girl is pure cornstarch, which is exactly what you need for the "Oogoo" method. Any brand of pure cornstarch acts as both a thickening agent and a "curing catalyst" when mixed with silicone.

How it Works

  • Internal Curing: 100% silicone typically cures by absorbing moisture from the air, which is why thick blobs often stay gooey in the middle for days. Cornstarch naturally holds microscopic amounts of water; when you mix it in, you are essentially "seeding" the silicone with moisture from the inside out, causing it to harden evenly in minutes.
  • Texture Control: Adding the starch transforms the runny silicone into a moldable dough. This allows you to shape it by hand or press it into a mold without it sagging or running.

Pro-Tips for Your First Batch

  • The Ratio: Start with a 1:1 ratio by volume. You can adjust this as you go: more cornstarch makes a stiffer, faster-curing rubber, while less starch keeps it softer and more flexible.
  • Work Surface: Use a piece of wax paper or a silicone baking mat as your mixing surface. The putty won't stick to these, making cleanup much easier.
  • Gloves are Key: Even though the starch makes the silicone less messy, it is still incredibly sticky until it begins to "set." Nitrile gloves will save you from having to scrub your hands with mineral spirits later.
  • Coloring: If you want your parts to be a specific color, add a single drop of oil-based paint or a tiny pinch of powdered pigment during the mixing phase. Since Clabber Girl is white, it will naturally turn the clear silicone into an opaque, matte finish.
